front: Who gains and who loses from unexpected inflation?
back: Gain: borrowers on fixed-rate loans; those whose incomes rise faster than prices. Lose: savers, lenders, people on fixed incomes, workers whose wages lag behind prices.
Nominal interest rate − rate of inflation

front: Which function of money fails first in high inflation?
back: Store of value: money held loses its purchasing power.

front: Give two monetary measures to reduce inflation.
back: Raise interest rates; slow the growth of the money supply (or allow the currency to appreciate).

front: Give two fiscal measures to reduce inflation.
back: Cut government spending; raise direct taxes (reduce the deficit, and stop financing it by creating money).

front: How do supply-side policies reduce inflation?
back: They raise productivity and capacity, lowering unit costs, so output can grow without prices rising.

front: Why is cost-push inflation hard to cure by cutting demand?
back: Cutting demand lowers inflation only by reducing output and raising unemployment, which are already suffering.

front: How does high inflation harm the economy as a whole?
back: Uncertainty reduces investment; exports become less competitive; income is redistributed unfairly; menu and shoe-leather costs.
